idiom_name: module-level const (ES module evaluation, once) / memoized accessor
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's module semantics: a module body is evaluated once per module instance and its top-level const bindings are initialized then, so the shared instance is a module-level const or a class with a private constructor reached through a static getter (the handbook covers both ES module and CommonJS forms). For deferred construction use the same memoized accessor as JavaScript; type-only constructs (interface, type alias, `import type`, declare) are erased and therefore cannot themselves serve as an initialization point. There is no guard object to write - the only real question is which module registry owns the instance.
pitfalls: `import type` and other erased constructs do not evaluate the module, so a module imported only for its types never runs its top-level initialization - a trap when that top-level code was supposed to construct the shared value.
Module identity strikes again: mixed CJS/ESM output, bundler duplication or two copies of a package in node_modules can produce two instances whose types still look identical to the checker.
Circular imports yield temporal-dead-zone errors or undefined values at runtime that the type checker cannot see; keep module-level initialization dependency-free or push it behind an accessor.

The memoized accessor is not protected against concurrent first use - JavaScript threads do not share memory, but worker_threads and re-entrant async code can each build their own copy - and a rejected initializer promise should not be cached unless that is intended.
